newsitem.title: USA: U.S. tobacco talks continuing in Chicago.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tobacco talks continuing in Chicago.

text.p: Milestone talks between cigarette maker executives and anti-tobacco leaders continued Sunday in Chicago, but the lead negotiator for states sueing the tobacco companies said it will probably be tough to reach a completely satisfactory agreement.

"We have a lot of demands, and I'm not sure if they're going to adhere to the demands that we've asked them for," said Mississippi Attorney General Michael Moore on ABC television's "This Week" program on Sunday.

Speaking from Chicago where he said he was heading back to the talks immediately after the program, Moore said the main objective of the talks is not really about money, but an effort to get tobacco companies to change the way they do business and "to tell the truth about their product."

Moore said that negotiators have spent most of their time talking about tobacco's impact on public health and the issue of children smoking, and very little time on the amount of money that cigarette makers will agree to pay to compensate victioms of tobacco smoking.

"All this talk about money and immunity and those things -- we spend about 80 percent of our time at the table talking about public health and children ... and frankly we haven't even gotten to those issues that people seem to be focusing on," he said.

The talks began behind closed doors about two weeks ago between top industry executives and an array of anti-tobacco leaders. Published reports have said the industry might pay as much as $300 billion over 25 years into a compensation fund for smokers who fall sick with lung cancer and other diseases.
In return, the tobacco industry would get broad shelter from lawsuits and higher stock market valuations on their thriving tobacco and non-smoking businesses.

Asked if he thought $300 billion was enough for the cigarette makers to pay out, Moore said, "I don't think there's enough money in this world frankly to pay for the damage that the tobacco companies have done in the past and the damage that they will do in the future. So this settlement or resolution can't be just about money -- it's got to be about marked change in the way this industry does business, and what we can do in the future."

News of the talks cheered Wall Street and has boosted the stocks of tobacco companies on speculation that a comprehensive settlement was imminent. The tobacco industry has steadfastly fought lawsuits and restrictions on its products.
